t: External merge sort for oversized archives
title: External merge sort for oversized archives
description: External merge sort sorts data bigger than RAM by sorting disk-sized runs and then k-way merging them. The input is read in memory-sized chunks, each sorted and spilled as a run file; a tournament-tree merge then repeatedly emits the smallest head across all runs. Only one block per run stays in memory, so terabytes sort in gigabytes. Use it to sort archive datasets that dwarf available memory.
demo:
import heapq, tempfile, os
runs, d = [], tempfile.mkdtemp()
data = list(range(1000, 0, -1))
for i in range(0, len(data), 250):
    p = os.path.join(d, f"run{i}"); open(p, "w").write("\n".join(map(str, sorted(data[i:i+250])))); runs.append(p)
merged = list(heapq.merge(*[map(int, open(p)) for p in runs]))
print("sorted:", merged[:3], "...", merged[-3:])
assert merged == sorted(data)
import shutil; shutil.rmtree(d)

t: Replacement selection for long sorted runs
title: Replacement selection for long sorted runs
description: Replacement selection builds initial sorted runs averaging twice memory size by always emitting the smallest available record. Records stream through a memory heap; the smallest is emitted, and its replacement joins the current run only if larger than the last emitted — otherwise it waits for the next run. Longer runs mean fewer merge passes. Use it to cut merge passes when sorting large archives.
demo:
import heapq
stream = [5, 1, 4, 2, 8, 0, 9, 3, 7, 6]
mem = 4
heap = stream[:mem]; heapq.heapify(heap)
rest, waiting, runs, cur, last = stream[mem:], [], [], [], float("-inf")
while heap or rest or waiting:
    while heap:
        x = heapq.heappop(heap)
        if x >= last: cur.append(x); last = x
        else: waiting.append(x)          # belongs to the next run
        if rest: heapq.heappush(heap, rest.pop(0))
    runs.append(cur); cur, last = [], float("-inf")
    heap, waiting = waiting, []; heapq.heapify(heap)
print("runs:", runs, "| first run length:", len(runs[0]), "= 2x memory" if len(runs[0]) == 2*mem else "")
assert all(r == sorted(r) for r in runs)
assert sorted(sum(runs, [])) == sorted(stream)

title: K-way tournament merge
description: A tournament tree merges k sorted runs by replaying matches only along the winner's path, costing O(log k) per emitted record. Leaves hold run heads; each internal node holds the smaller of its children, and the root is the global minimum. After emitting, only the winner's leaf refills and replays upward — far cheaper than scanning all k heads. Use it as the merge engine inside external sorts.
demo:
import heapq
runs = [[1, 9], [2, 8], [3, 7]]
out = list(heapq.merge(*runs))  # heapq.merge is a tournament-style k-way merge
print("tournament merge:", out)
assert out == [1, 2, 3, 7, 8, 9]

title: Iterator pipelines with constant memory
description: Iterator pipelines chain lazy generators so each archive record flows through all stages with only one record in flight. Python generators yield one item at a time; map/filter stages compose without materializing lists, holding memory flat regardless of input size. The pipeline processes unbounded archives in bounded RAM. Use it for ETL over archives far larger than memory.

title: Windowed streaming aggregation
description: Windowed aggregation maintains running statistics over a sliding window of the archive stream without storing history. A deque holds the current window; each arrival appends and each departure subtracts, keeping sum, count, and average in O(1) amortized time. Tumbling and sliding windows both reduce to bounded queues. Use it for live archive metrics like ingest rate and average record size.
demo:
from collections import deque
win, total = deque(), 0
avgs = []
for x in [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]:
    win.append(x); total += x
    if len(win) > 3: total -= win.popleft()
    avgs.append(total / len(win))
print("window avgs:", avgs)
assert avgs[-1] == 40.0

title: Reservoir sampling of archive streams
description: Reservoir sampling keeps a uniform random sample of k records from a stream of unknown length in O(k) memory. The first k records fill the reservoir; record i (i>k) replaces a random reservoir slot with probability k/i, which keeps every record's inclusion probability exactly k/n. One pass, fixed memory, unbiased sample. Use it to sample huge archive streams for profiling and testing.
demo:
import random
random.seed(42)
k, reservoir = 5, []
for i, x in enumerate(range(1000)):
    if i < k: reservoir.append(x)
    elif random.random() < k/(i+1): reservoir[random.randrange(k)] = x
print("sample:", sorted(reservoir))
assert len(reservoir) == 5 and len(set(reservoir)) == 5

title: HyperLogLog cardinality estimation
description: HyperLogLog estimates the number of distinct archive values in kilobytes of memory with about 2% error. Each value hashes to a register by its leading-zero count; the harmonic mean of 2^register across m registers estimates cardinality, with bias corrections for small and huge ranges. It counts billions of distinct IDs in 12KB. Use it for distinct counts (unique terms, visitors) over massive archives.
demo:
import hashlib
m = 64
regs = [0]*m
def add(v):
    h = int(hashlib.md5(str(v).encode()).hexdigest(), 16)
    r = h % m; w = (h // m)
    regs[r] = max(regs[r], (w & -w).bit_length())
for i in range(1000): add(f"doc-{i}")
import math
est = 0.7213/(1+1.079/m) * m*m / sum(2.0**-r for r in regs)
print("estimate vs true 1000:", round(est))
assert 700 < est < 1400

title: Count-Min sketch for frequency estimation
description: A Count-Min sketch estimates how often each archive key appears using a small table of counters with hash collisions. d hash functions map each key to one counter per row; increments touch all d counters and queries take the minimum, which bounds overcounting. Error is at most epsilon*N with probability 1-delta for width 2/epsilon. Use it for heavy-hitter detection in archive streams.
demo:
import hashlib
w, d = 64, 3
table = [[0]*w for _ in range(d)]
def hs(k): return [int(hashlib.md5(f"{k}{i}".encode()).hexdigest(), 16) % w for i in range(d)]
for _ in range(50):
    for h, row in zip(hs("mars"), table): row[h] += 1
for _ in range(5):
    for h, row in zip(hs("venus"), table): row[h] += 1
est = min(row[h] for h, row in zip(hs("mars"), table))
print("estimated count of 'mars':", est, "(true 50)")
assert 50 <= est < 70

title: T-digest style quantile sketching
description: Quantile sketches estimate medians and percentiles of archive streams in tiny memory by merging nearby values into weighted centroids. Incoming values join the nearest centroid or start new ones; periodic compression merges close centroids while keeping more detail near the tails (q near 0 or 1). Queries interpolate across centroids for any quantile. Use it for latency and size percentiles over archive operations.

title: Spill-to-disk threshold management
description: Spill management monitors a processing buffer and flushes it to disk sorted runs before memory is exhausted. The engine tracks bytes used against a budget; crossing the high-water mark sorts and spills the buffer, then continues with freed memory. Spills are transparent to downstream merge stages. Use it to keep hash aggregations and sorts safe under fixed memory.
demo:
budget, buf, spills = 5, [], 0
for x in [3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6]:
    buf.append(x)
    if len(buf) >= budget:
        buf = sorted(buf); spills += 1; buf = []
print("spills:", spills, "| leftover:", buf)
assert spills == 1

t: LRU eviction cache for hot archive records
title: LRU eviction cache for hot archive records
description: An LRU cache keeps the most recently used archive records in memory and evicts the least recently used when full. A hash map plus doubly-linked list (or OrderedDict) gives O(1) get/put with recency updates; eviction drops the tail. Hit rates soar when archive access follows temporal locality. Use it to cache hot archive records in front of slower storage.

t: Memory budget accounting per pipeline stage
title: Memory budget accounting per pipeline stage
description: Budget accounting assigns each pipeline stage a memory quota and refuses allocations that would breach it, failing gracefully instead of OOM-killing. Stages request bytes from a central accountant; grants deduct from the budget and releases credit back. Breaches trigger the stage's spill policy rather than a crash. Use it to run multi-stage archive pipelines safely on shared machines.
demo:
class Accountant:
    def __init__(s, total): s.total, s.used = total, 0
    def ask(s, n):
        if s.used + n <= s.total: s.used += n; return True
        return False
    def free(s, n): s.used -= n
a = Accountant(100)
print("ask 60:", a.ask(60), "| ask 50:", a.ask(50))
a.free(60); print("after free, ask 50:", a.ask(50))
assert a.used == 50

title: Bounded queue backpressure
description: Bounded queues cap inter-stage buffers so a fast producer blocks instead of flooding memory when the consumer lags. With maxsize set, put() blocks or raises when full; the producer naturally paces to the consumer's speed. Combined with monitoring, full queues pinpoint the slow stage. Use it between every stage of a memory-bounded archive pipeline.
demo:
from queue import Queue, Full
q = Queue(maxsize=2)
q.put("a"); q.put("b")
try: q.put("c", block=False); overflow = False
except Full: overflow = True
print("third put blocked (Full raised):", overflow)
assert overflow and q.qsize() == 2

title: Chunked batching for steady memory
description: Chunked batching processes the archive in fixed-size batches, keeping peak memory proportional to the chunk, not the archive. The reader yields chunks of N records; each chunk is fully processed and released before the next loads. Throughput stays high while memory stays flat. Use it for any full-archive pass on a memory budget.

title: Memory-mapped streaming reads
description: Memory-mapped files let the OS page archive data in on demand, streaming huge files with almost no application memory. mmap exposes the file as a byte array; the kernel pages in only touched regions and evicts under pressure. Sequential scans stream at disk speed with a tiny resident set. Use it to scan multi-gigabyte archive files on small machines.
demo:
import mmap, os
p = "/tmp/t1_mmap.bin"
open(p, "wb").write(b"0123456789" * 100)
with open(p, "rb") as f:
    with mmap.mmap(f.fileno(), 0, access=mmap.ACCESS_READ) as m:
        total = sum(m[i] - 48 for i in range(len(m)))
print("digit sum over 1000 bytes:", total)
assert total == 100 * sum(range(10)) == 4500
os.remove(p)
print("mmap scan ok")
